last_change: Excluded Streamlit/Gradio layout blocks from nesting depth, switched to code-only line counting for god file detection, added monorepo config files to framework conventions

dimensions.name: Code Structure
dimensions.description: The biggest weight because it's the biggest AI tell. AI tools write everything into one file, one function, deeply nested. This dimension catches that.

checks.name: God Files
checks.description: Files that do too much. We count actual code lines — comments, blanks, and docstrings don't count. A 600-line file with 200 lines of comments is really a 400-line file.
exclusions: Test files, generated files, vendored code
Data files: locales, i18n, seed data, fixtures

checks.name: Deep Nesting
checks.description: Counts control flow nesting only — if/else/for/while/try/catch. Not object literals, not JSX structure, not config nesting. Single-line returns like `if (x) return y` don't count.
exclusions: Test files, generated files, data files

checks.name: Duplicate Files
checks.threshold: 3+ files with same base name and ≥50% content overlap
checks.description: Catches copy-paste patterns where the same logic lives in multiple places. Compares content similarity, not just file names.
exclusions: Monorepo config files expected to repeat across workspaces

dimensions.name: Error Handling
dimensions.description: AI-generated code loves to swallow errors. An empty catch block is a bug waiting to happen — we look for evidence that errors are actually being handled, not just silenced.

checks.name: Empty Catch Blocks
checks.threshold: Any catch block with no code inside
checks.description: A catch block that catches an error and does nothing with it. This is almost never what you want.

checks.name: Console-Only Error Handling
checks.threshold: Catch blocks that only console.log the error
checks.description: Logging an error isn't handling it. If the user can't tell something went wrong, you're just hiding problems.
exclusions: console.warn in catch blocks (assumed intentional graceful degradation)

checks.name: Console.log Density
checks.threshold: 5+ console.log calls in a single file
checks.description: A high density of console.log usually means debug code left behind in production. We're not counting console.warn or console.error — those are often intentional.
exclusions: Build config files (vite.config, webpack.config, next.config, etc.)

dimensions.name: Test Coverage
dimensions.description: Not whether your tests are good — we can't tell that from static analysis. But we can tell if they exist, and roughly how much of your code is covered.

checks.name: No Tests Found
checks.threshold: Zero test files in the entire repo
checks.description: We look for .test.*, .spec.*, test_*, and files in /test/ directories. If we find nothing, that's a critical finding.

checks.name: No Test Script
checks.threshold: Node.js project with no test script in package.json
checks.description: Even if test files exist, there should be a way to run them. We look for test, test:unit, test:e2e, and test:integration scripts.

checks.name: Low Test-to-Source Ratio
checks.description: Compares total lines of test code to total lines of source code. Below 10% means you're barely testing anything.

dimensions.name: Security
dimensions.description: We can't do a real security audit from static analysis, but we can catch the obvious disasters — committed secrets, hardcoded credentials, and .env files in the repo.

checks.name: .env File Committed
checks.threshold: Any .env file present in the repo
checks.description: If we can see your .env file, so can everyone else. This usually means secrets are exposed.

checks.name: Hardcoded Secrets
checks.threshold: API keys, passwords, tokens in source code
checks.description: Detects OpenAI keys (sk-...), GitHub tokens (ghp_...), AWS keys (AKIA...), and general api_key/password/secret assignments with string values.
exclusions: Placeholder values (your-password, example-key, test-secret, dummy_*, fake_*)
Example, sample, tutorial, and documentation directories
E2E setup scripts, seed files, fixtures, and mock data

dimensions.name: Dependencies
dimensions.description: Lower weight because dependency management is genuinely hard and sometimes you just need the packages. But we still flag obvious bloat and hygiene issues.

checks.name: Excessive Dependencies
checks.description: A high dependency count increases attack surface, bundle size, and the odds of supply chain issues.

checks.name: Missing Lock File
checks.threshold: Dependencies present but no lock file
checks.description: Without a lock file, every install might get different versions. We look for package-lock.json, yarn.lock, pnpm-lock.yaml, and bun.lockb.

checks.name: Duplicate-Purpose Packages
checks.threshold: 2+ packages that do the same thing
checks.description: Having both axios and node-fetch? Both moment and dayjs? Pick one. We check 8 categories: HTTP clients, utilities, dates, frameworks, test runners, loggers, validators, and CSS-in-JS.

dimensions.name: Documentation
dimensions.description: The lightest weight because docs are genuinely optional for small projects. But no README at all? That's a choice.

checks.name: No README
checks.threshold: No README.md file in the repo
checks.description: A repo without a README is a repo nobody can use. Even a few lines explaining what it does and how to run it is better than nothing.

checks.name: Thin README
checks.description: An auto-generated or placeholder README with just a title and nothing else. We want to see at least what it does and how to run it.

checks.name: Very Few Inline Comments
checks.threshold: Below 2% comment ratio in files with 200+ lines
checks.description: We're not looking for comments on every line. But a large file with almost no comments suggests the author didn't stop to explain any of the non-obvious logic.

skipped_files: node_modules, dist, build, .next, vendor, venv, and other dependency/output directories
Generated files (auto-generated headers, .d.ts declarations, .map files, migration files)
Lock files (package-lock.json, yarn.lock, etc.) — analyzed for presence, not content

optimization_process.name: Nightly Automated Stress Tests
optimization_process.description: Every night at 2am, an automated agent picks 5-10 diverse repos from GitHub — monorepos, framework-heavy apps, repos with generated code, data fixtures, and public API keys — runs them through every analyzer, reads the actual flagged code, and classifies each finding as legitimate or false positive. Pattern-fixable false positives get auto-fixed with test coverage, and a detailed report is generated. This runs every single night, so the rubric is always getting tighter.

optimization_process.name: False Positive Reports
optimization_process.description: Every finding on a report card has a flag button. When users report a false positive, we review it and, if confirmed, update the analyzer to handle that pattern. Real feedback from real repos drives real improvements.

optimization_process.name: Test-Gated Fixes
optimization_process.description: Every analyzer optimization must pass the full test suite before it ships. If a fix is too broad and breaks an existing test, it gets reverted automatically. No fix goes live without proof it doesn't create new problems.

optimization_process.name: Framework Awareness
optimization_process.description: Different frameworks have different conventions. Streamlit apps have deep nesting from layout blocks. Next.js repos have duplicated page.tsx files. Monorepos repeat config files. We teach the analyzer to understand these patterns instead of blindly flagging them.
